title: Program Testing and Maintenance
overview: This topic covers finding faults in a program, testing it methodically and keeping it useful after release. Paper 2 asks candidates to identify syntax, logic and run-time errors in given pseudocode and correct them, to dry-run an algorithm with a trace table, to name and describe testing methods (dry run, walkthrough, white-box, black-box, integration, alpha, beta, acceptance and stub), to choose normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary test data for a test plan, and to identify or carry out corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance, often by amending a given program. Answers score when an error is classified by its effect (will not translate, wrong result, or crash), when each testing method is described by who tests and what they can see, when test data comes with its expected result, and when a maintenance type is matched to the reason for the change.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of ways of exposing and avoiding faults in programs.
Locate and identify the different types of errors: syntax errors, logic errors and run-time errors.

Show understanding of the methods of testing available and select appropriate data for a given method, including dry run, walkthrough, white-box, black-box, integration, alpha, beta, acceptance and stub testing.
Show understanding of the need for a test strategy and test plan and their likely contents.
Choose appropriate test data for a test plan, including normal, abnormal and extreme/boundary data.
Show understanding of the need for continuing maintenance of a system and the differences between each type of maintenance: perfective, adaptive and corrective.
Analyse an existing program and make amendments to enhance functionality.

definitions.definition: An error in which a statement does not follow the grammar rules of the programming language, so the program cannot be translated. It is reported by the compiler or interpreter.
An error in the logic of the solution: the program runs, but it does not behave as intended and produces an incorrect result.
An error that occurs while the program is running and causes it to crash (stop unexpectedly) or freeze, for example dividing by zero or an infinite loop.
Working through an algorithm or program by hand, without a computer, recording the value of each variable and condition at each step in a trace table.
A table with a column for each variable (and for conditions and output) that records how their values change as an algorithm is dry-run.
Testing that uses knowledge of the program code, choosing test data so that every path through the code is executed and its results checked.
Testing that compares the actual results with the expected results for chosen inputs, worked out from the specification, without looking at the program code.
Testing the structure of a program before all modules are written, by using stubs: dummy modules whose body only outputs a message (or returns a fixed value) to show they were called.
Testing that individually tested modules work correctly together once they are combined into one program, usually adding one module at a time.

Alpha testing is done in-house by the developer's own testers. Beta testing is done by a limited number of chosen external users, in their own environments, before general release. Acceptance testing is done by the client, to check that bespoke software meets the requirements before they sign it off.
A detailed list of the tests to be carried out, giving for each test its purpose, the test data, the type of test data and the expected result, with space to record the actual result.

Corrective maintenance corrects errors found after the program is in use. Adaptive maintenance amends a program to enhance its functionality or respond to changed requirements or a changed environment. Perfective maintenance improves a program's performance or maintainability without changing what it does.

sections.title: Why faults occur, and ways of exposing and avoiding them
content: Software may not behave as expected for several reasons: a programmer makes a coding mistake, the requirements specification was drawn up wrongly, the designer makes a design error, a poorly designed interface leads users into mistakes, or the hardware fails. A fault that reaches the end user harms the developer's reputation, and the later a fault is found the more expensive it is to fix. So testing must happen throughout development, not only at the end.

Faults are exposed by testing: dry-running algorithms, reviewing code in walkthroughs, and running the program with carefully chosen test data. Testing can show that faults are present but can never prove that none remain, because a program cannot be tested with every possible input.

The best approach is to avoid faults in the first place. Most faults come from not fully understanding the problem, so a careful requirements analysis is essential. Faults are also reduced by using tried and tested design methods such as structured programming (small modules with clear interfaces, local variables and parameters), by following conventions such as meaningful identifiers, identifier tables and standard algorithms, and by reusing library modules that have already been tested.
bullets: Causes: coding mistakes, a wrong requirements specification, design errors, a poor user interface, hardware failure.
Expose faults: dry runs, walkthroughs, testing with chosen test data at every stage.
Avoid faults: thorough analysis, structured/modular design, conventions (meaningful identifiers, identifier tables), tested library modules.
Testing shows the presence of faults, never their absence; the earlier a fault is found, the cheaper it is to fix.

sections.title: Types of error: syntax, logic and run-time
content: A syntax error breaks the grammar rules of the language: a misspelt keyword, a missing bracket or quote, a missing ENDIF, or = used where the assignment arrow is needed. Syntax errors are the easiest to find because the translator reports them. Many editors underline them as the code is typed. A compiler checks the whole program, so a program that compiles has no syntax errors left. An interpreter only checks each statement as it is about to be executed, so a syntax error in a part of the program that has not yet been run can remain hidden. The error is sometimes reported on the line after the real mistake, because the translator only notices a problem when the next token is unexpected.

A logic error lets the program run but gives the wrong result: the wrong operator (< instead of <=, AND instead of OR), a loop that runs one time too many or too few, a variable initialised to the wrong value, or a calculation in the wrong order. The translator cannot detect these because the code is valid.

A run-time error happens while the program is executing and makes it crash or freeze: dividing by zero, using an array index outside the array's bounds, reading a file that does not exist, or an infinite loop. Logic and run-time errors can only be found by careful testing, and they are dangerous because they may only appear for particular data, so a program can seem to work for a long time before failing.
bullets: Syntax error: breaks the language rules; found by the compiler/interpreter; the program cannot be translated.
Logic error: the program runs but gives an incorrect result; found by testing and dry runs.
Run-time error: the program crashes or freezes during execution (division by zero, index out of range, missing file, infinite loop).
A compiled program has no syntax errors left; an interpreted one can still contain them in code that has not been run.

sections.title: Locating and correcting errors
content: To correct an error, first classify it by its effect, then find the line responsible. A syntax error message points close to the line. A logic error is found by comparing actual results with expected ones and then dry-running the code, or by using a debugger, to find where the values first go wrong. A run-time error is found by identifying the data that caused the crash and the statement being executed at the time.

When writing a correction in an exam, give the corrected line of code in full, not just a description, and check that the fix does not break anything else. The worked example has one error of each type.
bullets: Classify the error first: will not translate (syntax), wrong answer (logic), crash or freeze (run-time).
Locate: translator message for syntax; expected-versus-actual results plus a dry run for logic; the failing data for run-time.
Correct: rewrite the whole line, then re-test with the data that exposed the error.

examples.label: Worked example: one syntax, one logic and one run-time error
examples.content:
Intended: read marks until -1 is entered, then output the average mark.

01  DECLARE Total, Count, Mark : INTEGER
02  Total ← 0
03  Count ← 1
04  INPUT Mark
05  WHILE Mark <> -1
06     Total ← Total + Mark
07     Count ← Count + 1
08     INPUT Mark
09  ENDWHILE
10  OUTPUT "Average: , Total / Count

Syntax error, line 10: the closing quote is missing, so the string never ends.
   Correction: OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / Count

Logic error, line 03: Count starts at 1, so it ends one higher than the number
   of marks and the average is too small (see the trace in the dry-run section).
   Correction: Count ← 0

Run-time error, line 10 (after correcting line 03): if -1 is the first input,
   Count is 0 and the program divides by zero and crashes.
   Correction: replace line 10 with
      IF Count > 0 THEN
         OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / Count
      ELSE
         OUTPUT "No marks entered"
      ENDIF

sections.title: Stub testing
content: Stub testing lets the top-level structure of a program, such as a menu, be tested before all the modules it calls have been written. Each unfinished module is replaced by a stub: a procedure with the correct identifier whose body only outputs a message showing it was called, or a function that returns a fixed, known value.

Running the program then shows whether each menu choice or condition calls the right module in the right order. Each stub is later replaced by the real module and tested. Stub testing fits top-down development and the structure chart from 12.2: the upper levels are tested first, with stubs standing in for the lower levels.
bullets: A stub is a dummy module: it has the right identifier (and parameters) but only outputs a message or returns a fixed value.
Purpose: test the flow of control (which module is called when) before the modules are finished.
Stubs are replaced one at a time by the real, tested modules.

examples.label: A menu tested with stubs
examples.content:
PROCEDURE AddStudent()
   OUTPUT "AddStudent called"          // stub
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE FindStudent()
   OUTPUT "FindStudent called"         // stub
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION CountStudents() RETURNS INTEGER
   RETURN 3                            // stub returns a fixed value
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Choice : INTEGER
OUTPUT "1 Add  2 Find  3 Count"
INPUT Choice
CASE OF Choice
   1 : CALL AddStudent()
   2 : CALL FindStudent()
   3 : OUTPUT "Students: ", CountStudents()
   OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Not a menu option"
ENDCASE

// Test: input 2 should output "FindStudent called";
// input 3 should output "Students: 3"; input 7 should output "Not a menu option".

sections.title: Black-box and white-box testing
content: In black-box testing the tester cannot see the code, and it is often someone other than the programmer. Test data and expected results are worked out from the specification: what the program is supposed to do. The program is run, the actual results are recorded and compared with the expected ones. A difference shows a fault exists, but not where; a dry run or a debugger is then used to find the lines that need correcting.

In white-box testing the tester uses knowledge of the code to choose test data that makes every path through it run: both branches of every IF, every CASE clause, and each loop run zero times, once and several times. The exact values do not matter as long as together they reach every path. White-box testing is usually done by the programmer while modules are being written; black-box testing checks the program against its requirements.
The worked example shows the minimum white-box test data for a nested IF with three paths.
bullets: Black-box: code not visible; test data and expected results come from the specification; compares expected with actual results.
White-box: code visible; test data chosen so that every path (every branch and loop) is executed.
Black-box shows that a fault exists; white-box, dry runs and debuggers help locate it.

examples.label: Worked example: white-box test data for every path
examples.content:
IF Age < 16 THEN
   Price ← 5
ELSE
   IF Age >= 65 THEN
      Price ← 6
   ELSE
      Price ← 10
   ENDIF
ENDIF

There are three paths, so at least three tests are needed:

Test | Age | Age < 16 | Age >= 65 | Expected Price
1    | 10  | TRUE     | (not tested) | 5
2    | 70  | FALSE    | TRUE      | 6
3    | 30  | FALSE    | FALSE     | 10

Any values giving these condition results would do. To check the comparisons
themselves (< rather than <=, >= rather than >), add the values at each edge:
15 → 5, 16 → 10, 64 → 10, 65 → 6.

sections.title: Dry runs, trace tables and walkthroughs
content: A dry run checks an algorithm by hand. Draw a trace table with a column for every variable, one for each condition being tested and one for output. Work through the algorithm one statement at a time, writing a value only when it changes (a blank cell means the value is unchanged) and starting a new row for each pass of a loop. Numbering the lines, with a column for the line being executed, helps you follow the exact order. Comparing the final output with the expected result shows whether the algorithm is correct, and the rows show where it first goes wrong.

A walkthrough is a review in which the programmer steps through the algorithm or code, often with other people such as colleagues, explaining what each part does. The coursebook treats walking through with a trace table as another name for a dry run. Both are used early, while modules are being written, and they can be done before the program even exists as code.
bullets: Trace table: one column per variable, condition and output; enter a value only when it changes; one row per loop pass.
Dry run: find the expected output by hand and see where the actual values first go wrong.
Walkthrough: stepping through the code, often explaining it to others, to spot errors before or during coding.

examples.label: Worked example: a dry run that exposes the logic error
examples.content:
Dry run of the original average program (Count ← 1 on line 03)
with the inputs 10, 20, -1. Expected output: Average: 15

Mark | Total | Count | Mark <> -1 | OUTPUT
     | 0     | 1     |            |
10   |       |       | TRUE       |
     | 10    | 2     |            |
20   |       |       | TRUE       |
     | 30    | 3     |            |
-1   |       |       | FALSE      |
     |       |       |            | Average: 10

Actual output 10 ≠ expected 15. Only two marks were entered but Count is 3,
and the table shows Count was already 1 before any mark was read: line 03
is the fault. With Count ← 0 the final row gives 30 / 2 = 15.

sections.title: Integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing
content: Programs are usually made of many modules, sometimes written by different programmers. Each module can pass its own tests and still fail when combined, for example if the modules disagree about the order or type of parameters. Integration testing tests the modules together once they are joined, usually adding one module at a time and testing again before the next is added, so any new fault can be traced to the module just added.

Before release, software is alpha tested in-house by the developer's own testers, who try to find faults before anyone outside sees it. What happens next depends on who the software is for. Bespoke software, written for a particular client, goes to acceptance testing: the client tests it, often with real data, to confirm it does everything in the requirements specification. When it passes, the client signs it off as part of the hand-over. Software written for general sale has no single client, so after alpha testing a beta version is given to a limited number of chosen users, who use it in their own environments with their own hardware and data and report faults back so they can be fixed before general release.
bullets: Integration: combine separately tested modules and check they work together; add one module at a time.
Alpha: in-house testers at the developer, before anyone outside sees the software.
Beta: a limited number of chosen external users, in real environments, before general release; they report faults back.
Acceptance: the client checks bespoke software against the requirements before signing it off.

sections.title: Test strategy and test plan
content: A test strategy is decided during design. It sets out how the software will be tested: which testing methods suit the project, in what order they happen, and who carries them out. Planning this early means testing is rigorous from the start rather than improvised at the end.

Large programs cannot be tested exhaustively, so testing has to be systematic to find as many faults as possible. An outline test plan lists what needs checking: does each menu choice go to the correct module, is input validated, do loops and decisions work correctly, is data saved to the correct files, and are the results correct? This is then expanded into a detailed test plan, where each test has a number, a description of what it tests, the test data, the type of test data, the expected result and a column for the actual result. Writing the expected result before the test is run keeps the comparison honest, and a completed plan is a record of what has and has not been checked.
bullets: Test strategy: the overall approach (which methods, when, by whom), decided during design.
Test plan contents: test number, what is being tested, test data, type of data, expected result, actual result (and any action taken).
Need: programs cannot be tested exhaustively, so testing must be planned and systematic, and the results recorded.

sections.title: Choosing test data: normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary
content: Test data is chosen deliberately, unlike real data, so that each test checks a particular possibility. Normal (valid) data is typical data the program should accept and process correctly. Abnormal (erroneous) data is data the program should reject: values outside the allowed range, the wrong data type, or missing input. Extreme data is the largest and smallest values that are still valid, at each end of the normal range. Boundary data tests each edge of the range from both sides: the value just within the limit, which must be accepted, and the value just outside it, which must be rejected.

Use a separate test for each kind of abnormal value. A single value that is wrong in two ways, such as a negative decimal, does not show which check is working. Boundary tests matter because the most common logic error in validation is a comparison off by one, such as < where <= was needed, and only values at the edge reveal it.
Always give the expected result with each item of test data. The worked example is a test plan for a ticket-booking input where the number of tickets must be a whole number from 1 to 10 inclusive.
bullets: Normal: typical valid data, should be accepted.
Abnormal (erroneous): invalid data such as out of range, wrong type or missing, should be rejected.
Extreme: the largest and smallest valid values, should be accepted.
Boundary: values on either side of each limit: just inside (accept) and just outside (reject).
Test one kind of invalid value at a time, and state the expected result for every test.

examples.label: Worked example: test plan for 1 to 10 tickets
examples.content:
Rule: the number of tickets must be a whole number from 1 to 10 inclusive.

No. | Test data | Type                  | Expected result | Actual result
1   | 4         | Normal                | Accepted        | Accepted
2   | 7         | Normal                | Accepted        | Accepted
3   | 1         | Extreme / boundary    | Accepted        | Accepted
4   | 10        | Extreme / boundary    | Accepted        | Rejected  ← fault
5   | 0         | Boundary (just below) | Rejected        | Rejected
6   | 11        | Boundary (just above) | Rejected        | Rejected
7   | -5        | Abnormal              | Rejected        | Rejected
8   | 2.5       | Abnormal (not whole)  | Rejected        | Rejected
9   | "three"   | Abnormal (not number) | Rejected        | Rejected
10  | (blank)   | Abnormal (missing)    | Rejected        | Rejected

Test 4 fails: 10 is valid but was rejected. The upper check was most likely
written Tickets < 10 instead of Tickets <= 10. Only a test at the edge could
reveal this: 4 and 7 pass either way. After correcting the line, test 4
(and test 6, to check 11 is still rejected) must be run again.

sections.title: The need for continuing maintenance and its three types
content: A program does not wear out like a machine, but it still needs changing after it has been released. Faults appear that testing missed, often because a rarely used part of the program is finally run or unusual data is entered. Users' needs change, the law changes, or the program must run on new hardware or a new operating system. And a working program can often be made faster or easier to maintain. Maintenance keeps the program correct and useful for as long as it is in use.

Corrective maintenance corrects errors, logic or run-time, that come to light while the program is in use. The programmer uses a trace table or debugging software to find the cause. A correction can introduce a new error, so the program must be tested again afterwards.

Adaptive maintenance amends a program to enhance its functionality or to respond to changes in the specification, for example adding a new feature the users now need, changing it for a new tax law, or making it work on a new platform. Perfective maintenance improves a program that already works correctly, making it faster or more efficient (for example changing file access from sequential to direct) or easier to maintain (clearer identifiers, comments, repeated code moved into a subroutine), without changing what it does.
bullets: Why maintenance is needed: faults missed in testing, changing requirements or laws, new hardware or software, room for improvement.
Corrective: fix errors found during use.
Adaptive: change what the program does, to enhance functionality or meet new or changed requirements.
Perfective: improve performance or maintainability without changing what the program does.
Classify by the reason for the change, not by how big the change is; re-test after any maintenance.

sections.title: Analysing an existing program and making amendments
content: To amend an existing program, first read and dry-run it until you understand what each variable holds and what each part does. Then decide exactly what the new requirement changes, make the smallest set of changes that meets it (new variables declared, conditions added, outputs extended), and keep the existing style and identifiers. Finally, test again with test data that checks both the new behaviour and the old behaviour, which must not have been broken.

The worked example is adaptive maintenance on the corrected average program. Two new requirements are added: marks outside 0 to 100 must be rejected with a message, and the highest mark must be output as well as the average.
bullets: Understand first: read and dry-run the existing code.
Change only what the new requirement needs, and declare any new variables.
Re-test the new behaviour and the original behaviour.

examples.label: Worked example: the average program amended to validate marks and find the highest
examples.content:
DECLARE Total, Count, Mark, Highest : INTEGER     // Highest is new
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
Highest ← -1                                      // new: below any valid mark
INPUT Mark
WHILE Mark <> -1
   IF Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100 THEN              // new: validation
      Total ← Total + Mark
      Count ← Count + 1
      IF Mark > Highest THEN                      // new: track the highest
         Highest ← Mark
      ENDIF
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Mark rejected: must be 0 to 100"   // new
   ENDIF
   INPUT Mark
ENDWHILE
IF Count > 0 THEN
   OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / Count
   OUTPUT "Highest: ", Highest                   // new
ELSE
   OUTPUT "No marks entered"
ENDIF

// Test: inputs 40, 150, 70, -1
// 150 is rejected with the message; Total = 110, Count = 2
// Output: Average: 55   Highest: 70
// Test: input -1 only → No marks entered (the original behaviour still works)

diagram.title: Testing from first module to release
nodes: Design: test strategy and test plan drawn up
Writing modules: dry runs, walkthroughs, white-box and stub testing
Joining modules: integration testing, one module at a time
Whole program: black-box testing, then alpha testing in-house

analysisChains.title: Classifying an error from its symptoms
steps: A program that finds the mean journey time translates and runs, and gives correct answers for most test data
When a user enters no journeys at all, the program stops with an error message part-way through
It could be translated, so this is not a syntax error; it stopped rather than giving a wrong answer, so it is not only a logic error
The mean is calculated as Total / Count, and with no journeys Count is 0, so the program divides by zero
analysisChains.evaluation: It is a run-time error, exposed only by one particular input, which is why it survived normal testing. The correction is to test IF Count > 0 before dividing and output a suitable message otherwise, and the plan should include a test with no data.

analysisChains.title: Choosing alpha, beta or acceptance testing
steps: A company writes a stock-control system for one particular chain of shops and has finished its own in-house (alpha) testing
The software is bespoke: it was written for one client from that client's requirements specification
Beta testing is for software written for general sale, where there is no single client and the developer needs feedback from varied real users
Here the client must confirm the system meets the agreed requirements before hand-over
analysisChains.evaluation: The next stage is acceptance testing by the shop chain, using their own data, ending in sign-off. Beta testing would suit the same company's general-sale product instead, because it needs many users' environments to expose faults the in-house testers could not reproduce.

analysisChains.title: Identifying the type of maintenance
steps: A school's reporting program works correctly, but producing reports for 2000 students takes too long because each student's record is found by reading the file from the start
The programmer changes the file access from sequential to direct, and the reports come out the same, only faster
Nothing was wrong, so it is not corrective; the program does nothing new and meets no new requirement, so it is not adaptive
The change improves performance while keeping the same behaviour
analysisChains.evaluation: This is perfective maintenance. If the school then asked for each report to include attendance figures, that would be adaptive maintenance (new functionality), and fixing a report that showed the wrong grade would be corrective. The type depends on the reason for the change, not its size.

examTips: When asked to identify an error type, justify it by its effect: a syntax error stops translation, a logic error gives a wrong result, a run-time error makes the program crash or freeze.
When correcting pseudocode, write out the whole corrected statement, keeping the identifiers used in the question.
For each item of test data give its type and the expected result; for a range, include both extreme values and a value just outside each limit.

Distinguish testing methods by who does the testing and what they can see: code (white-box) or only the specification (black-box); in-house (alpha), chosen external users (beta) or the client (acceptance).
In a trace table, only enter a value when it changes, start a new row for each loop pass, and include the output column.
commonMistakes: Calling division by zero a logic error: it makes the program crash, so it is a run-time error.
Saying black-box testing means the tester does not know what the program should do; they do not see the code, but they use the specification.
Confusing beta testing (external users, software for general sale) with acceptance testing (the client, bespoke software).
Giving test data without an expected result, or choosing boundary values that are well inside the range.
Testing two kinds of invalid value with one item of data, such as a negative decimal, so a pass or fail does not show which check worked.
Describing adaptive maintenance as fixing bugs, or perfective maintenance as adding new features; bugs are corrective, new functionality is adaptive.
Amending a program without re-testing the original behaviour, so a new fault goes unnoticed.

quickRecall.question: Name the three types of error and how each shows itself.
quickRecall.answer: Syntax error: breaks the language rules, so the program will not translate. Logic error: runs but gives a wrong result. Run-time error: crashes or freezes during execution.

quickRecall.question: Why can a syntax error remain in an interpreted program but not a compiled one?
quickRecall.answer: A compiler checks every statement before running, whereas an interpreter only checks a statement when it is about to execute it, so errors in code that has not been run stay hidden.

quickRecall.question: Give three ways of avoiding faults in programs.
quickRecall.answer: Thorough requirements analysis; tried and tested design methods such as structured/modular programming; conventions such as meaningful identifiers and identifier tables; reusing tested library modules.

quickRecall.question: What is a stub and why is it used?
quickRecall.answer: A dummy module with the correct identifier whose body only outputs a message or returns a fixed value; it lets the program's structure and flow of control be tested before all modules are written.

quickRecall.question: Distinguish white-box from black-box testing.
quickRecall.answer: White-box uses the code and chooses data to test every path; black-box does not look at the code and compares actual with expected results worked out from the specification.

quickRecall.question: What is integration testing?
quickRecall.answer: Testing that separately tested modules work correctly together when combined, usually adding one module at a time.

quickRecall.question: Who carries out alpha, beta and acceptance testing?
quickRecall.answer: Alpha: in-house testers at the developer. Beta: a limited number of chosen external users before general release. Acceptance: the client, for bespoke software, before sign-off.

quickRecall.question: What does a test plan contain?
quickRecall.answer: For each test: a number, what is being tested, the test data, the type of test data, the expected result and the actual result.

quickRecall.question: For whole numbers 1 to 10 inclusive, give extreme and boundary test data.
quickRecall.answer: Extreme: 1 and 10 (accepted). Boundary: 1 and 0 at the lower limit, 10 and 11 at the upper limit; 0 and 11 must be rejected.

quickRecall.question: Define corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance.
quickRecall.answer: Corrective: fixing errors found in use. Adaptive: amending the program to enhance functionality or meet changed requirements. Perfective: improving performance or maintainability without changing what it does.
